learning.title: Learning log
learning.subtitle: A shelf for the things I have learned, am learning, and still want to learn.
learning.intro: This folder is for the wider life of curiosity. I want it to eventually hold one hundred things I have learned, am learning, or still hope to learn — from cycling and cooking to speedcubing, pen spinning, web development, languages, and practical everyday skills. It is less a polished expertise page than an honest map of how I keep becoming.

sections.title: Why this folder exists
sections.body: I do not like the idea that learning ends when coursework ends. Some of the most useful things in my life were learned sideways: how to ask better questions, how to cycle through a city, how to edit a sentence without flattening its voice, how to keep trying after being bad at something for a while. This page is for that slower education.

literature.title: Literature, Language & Theories
literature.subtitle: On why we read, how languages open archives, and why narrative theory matters for journalism.
literature.intro: I came to media studies through literature. My undergraduate years at the University of Dhaka were spent inside English departments and little magazines, reading postcolonial fiction and narrative theory. Language learning is not separate from this — each new language opens a different archive of thought. Spanish gave me Bolaño and a Colombian journalist whose English was exquisite but whose Spanish was a whole other octave. This folder holds the books, essays, languages, and theories that still shape how I think about truth, narrative, and attention.

sections.title: A memory
sections.body: 2022. Presiding over the English Department Art and Literary Club at Dhaka University. We organised a weekly chai o kobita reading circle — Bangla poems in one hand, tea-stained photocopies of Seamus Heaney in the other. I learned more about cadence and silence in those evenings than in any seminar.

spanish.intro: I fell in love with Spanish late — through Bolaño, through Almodóvar, through a trip I haven't taken yet. Tracking my progress honestly, including the plateaus.

sections.title: Why Spanish
sections.body: The short answer: I want to read 2666 in the original Spanish before I turn 30. The longer answer involves a Colombian journalist I interviewed in 2024 whose phrasing in English was exquisite but whose Spanish — I could tell from a single voice note — was a whole other octave. I wanted to hear her properly.

film.title: Film aesthetics
film.subtitle: On cinema as a way of looking, not just watching.
film.intro: Film has been my second education. I keep a running log of what I watch and what it taught me about framing, pacing, and truth.

sections.title: The frame that changed me
sections.body: Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali — the scene where Apu and Durga see the train cut across the kaash flowers. I was fourteen, watching on a borrowed DVD with a scratched surface. The screen would stutter every few frames. Somehow that made it more real. It was the first time I understood that cinema could be a way of remembering things that had not yet happened.

photography.title: Photography & travel
photography.subtitle: Quiet frames from the places I get to stand still in.
photography.intro: I carry a Fujifilm X100V everywhere. Most of what I shoot I never publish. This folder is for the few I come back to — and for the trips behind them.

sections.title: A photograph I haven't shared
sections.body: A boy sleeping on a stack of newspapers outside the Paltan press market, 4:30 AM, November 2023. I was on an assignment about night-shift printers. I took one frame and put the camera down. It felt rude to take a second. Sometimes the ethics of the picture you don't take is more interesting than the one you do.

community.title: Community education
community.subtitle: Teaching, translating, and passing things along.
community.intro: Some of the most meaningful work I've done happens outside the newsroom — counselling students, editing SOPs for free, running OSINT workshops for fact-checkers. This folder gathers those threads.

sections.title: Why I do this
sections.body: In 2019, a junior from my village in Kishoreganj showed me his IELTS speaking practice recording. He had memorised every answer word-for-word. His accent was perfect. His confidence was a performance. I realised most of our education system rewards that performance. So I started spending evenings helping students actually think in English rather than recite in it. That habit has never really stopped.

philosophy.title: Philosophy & Maths
philosophy.subtitle: The slow questions and the precise ones — logic, ethics, probability, and the structures underneath both.
philosophy.intro: Journalism throws up ethical puzzles every week. I've found that the tools to sit with them properly come from two places: philosophy, which teaches you to be precise about premises and consequences, and mathematics, which teaches you to be honest about uncertainty. I'm a serious amateur in both — building a reading group habit in philosophy and working through probability and graph theory on the maths side.

sections.title: The question I keep failing to answer
sections.body: Is it ethical to publish a verified story if you know the algorithm will only amplify the first, most inflammatory paragraph? I've sat with this since 2023. It shapes how I now structure leads. It has not made me a faster writer. It has, I hope, made me a more honest one.

running.title: Running log
running.subtitle: Endurance, discipline, and the clean little happiness of finishing a run.
running.intro: Running gives the mind a different kind of order. It is not glamorous, which is exactly why it helps: lace up, go out, come back a little steadier. This folder is for pace notes, routes, and the ordinary discipline of showing up.

sections.title: Why it belongs here
sections.body: Running is one of the few habits that cannot be performed into existence. You either went out or you did not. I like that honesty.

newness.title: Exploring newness
newness.subtitle: New food, new places, new people — every person is a story.
newness.intro: I travel to be made unfamiliar. When I land somewhere I haven't been, three things keep me honest: try a dish I can't pronounce, walk a street that doesn't end at the hotel, and let one stranger talk longer than the conversation politely calls for. Newness isn't an aesthetic for me; it's a way of staying interested in the world. The reporting habit started here. So did most of the friendships I still keep.

items.meta: Whatever the table near me is having — start there.
The alley behind the famous street is usually where the place actually lives.
One real conversation is worth more than five photographs.

sections.title: Why every person is a story
sections.body: On a long bus ride I once asked the man next to me what he did. He said he repaired sewing machines in three districts and had seen every model since 1978. He spoke for an hour. I learned how a small spring works, how a town's tailoring economy shifted after the floods, and why he insisted his daughter learn English. I had boarded that bus to get somewhere. I got off having reported a story I never wrote down. After that I stopped treating strangers like background.

history.title: History & Geopolitics
history.subtitle: How the present got here — and what the map of power actually looks like.
history.intro: I read history the way I read good journalism: as a method for understanding causation without collapsing complexity. South Asian history, the Cold War's long shadow over the Global South, the British Empire's archival traces in current media structures, and the geopolitics of the Indian Ocean — these are the threads I keep pulling. Geopolitics is not background reading. For anyone writing about platform power, algorithmic governance, or digital rights in Bangladesh, it is the context.

sections.title: Why this started
sections.body: In 2022, covering the Ukrainian crisis for TBS, I kept encountering readers who had no framework for why NATO expansion mattered or why Bangladesh's position was what it was. I started reading geopolitics properly then — not as ideology, but as geography, history, and interest. Three years later I can't report on digital policy without it.
